Subject: Access path evaluation: VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN for Acme Corp

Hi Jared / NetOps team,

Thanks again for the call this week. Per our discussion we're putting together a short evaluation to decide which connectivity pattern makes the most sense for the initial private deployment of Redwood Private in your environment. The three options we're evaluating: VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site (S2S) VPN to a customer-managed gateway.

Quick constraints you mentioned on the call:
- No cross-account VPC peering into production VPCs without security sign-off
- On-prem firewall is strict; only a few outbound ports allowed
- Strong preference for predictable egress IPs and flow-level logging for audit

Attached is a draft connectivity_matrix.xlsx with a rough pros/cons + rough cost/latency expectations. Request from our side before we finalize a recommendation:
1) Confirm whether cross-account peering is a flat no for production, or if exceptions are possible with an approval flow.
2) Provide the list of allowed outbound IP ranges + firewall contact (we'll need to open specific ports for POC).
3) Give approximate steady-state qps and SLA (p50/p95) requirements for the Redwood endpoint.

My initial thought: run a short POC over S2S VPN (fast to stand up, low risk) then migrate to PrivateLink for production if you want the endpoint to be private and provider-controlled. But I'll let Karthik and Rishi weigh in on operational tradeoffs.

Next steps: once we have the firewall/IAM constraints we can propose a short 10-day POC plan and a production rollout path.

Thanks,

Hi Monica,

Thanks for the summary — a few clarifications from our side:
- Cross-account peering into our prod VPCs is a non-starter for now. We can evaluate peering into a shared services or transit VPC but that would require significant change controls.
- Firewall team only allows outbound TCP 443 and a small set of management ports to specific CIDR ranges. I'll attach the allowed ranges separately.
- Expected steady-state: ~120–180 requests/sec (we saw peaks up to 220 in test), latency target for inference is p95 < 120ms.

PrivateLink looks appealing from a security posture perspective since we can keep traffic off the internet, but we worry about the cost and whether we can manage the NLBs for the interface endpoints. A temporary S2S VPN for the POC sounds good.

Subject: Re: Access path evaluation: VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN for Acme Corp

Hi all — quick technical breakdown (summary bullets rather than a long doc):

1) VPC Peering
- Pros: Low-latency, fully routed at L3, no managed endpoints on Redwood side. Lower data transfer overhead in same region.
- Cons: Cross-account peering into prod is policy-blocked here. Peering doesn't support transitive routing; you'd need a transit VPC or AWS Transit Gateway to reach other VPCs. No enforced endpoint semantics (harder to audit per-service).
- Operational notes: Requires route table entries on both sides; NAT if private IP overlap; flow logs are from VPC flow; egress IPs are not fixed (depends on NAT setup).

2) PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints)
- Pros: Strong isolation; only specific service ports are exposed; customer initiates connection to an interface endpoint in their VPC so we don't get inbound peering. Fixed ENI IPs in customer subnets -> predictable flows and simpler firewall rules. Supports per-endpoint IAM policies.
- Cons: Higher per-hour cost (ENIs / endpoint-hour) and per-GB data processing charges on AWS side. Requires NLB + TLS termination strategy; health checks need to be carefully configured for autoscaling.
- Operational notes: Egress IPs are predictable (ENI addresses), easier for audit. Slightly more complex to scale across AZs (need NLB + target groups) but is production-friendly.

3) Site-to-Site VPN
- Pros: Fast to stand up for POC, lower immediate cost, predictable IPsec tunnels -> simple firewall rules. Works with on-prem firewalls.
- Cons: Throughput and latency depend on VPN endpoints and on-prem network; less native visibility than PrivateLink. Requires keepalives and monitoring; stateful failure modes can be tricky.
- Operational notes: Good short-term POC approach. For long-term, if you need provider-controlled private endpoints and per-service access control, PrivateLink is preferable.

Recommendation:
- POC: S2S VPN for 10–14 days to validate traffic profile and latency at your scale.
- Production: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) unless Acme prefers to accept the operational burden of maintaining an NLB + peering fabric.

I'll update the connectivity_matrix.xlsx with these notes and rough cost delta estimates.

Jared — attaching a short S2S config snippet and a diagram for the proposed POC. High-level items included:
- S2S IPsec tunnels (primary + standby) terminating to our customer gateway IPs.
- BGP optional; we recommend static routing for the POC to keep firewall rules simpler.
- Suggested ports: TCP/443 (application), UDP 500/4500 and protocol 50 for IPsec (if using ASA), plus TCP 22 for initial management if your firewall team wants to peer.
- IP ranges: for POC, we recommend allowing the following ENI/NAT egress CIDRs from Redwood test accounts: 10.18.240.0/22, 52.15.33.128/26 (these are example ranges; prod ranges will be published with the deployment runbook).
- HA: deploy 3 AZ-backed endpoints on our side for failover when we move to PrivateLink.

I'll paste a short S2S snippet here for your firewall:
<BEGIN SNIPPET>
peer: 198.51.100.12
ike-version: 2
ike-enc: aes256-sha2_256
esp-enc: aes256-sha2_256
local-subnet: 10.240.0.0/16
remote-subnet: 10.18.240.0/22
keepalive: 30s
<END SNIPPET>

We'll also upload the full terraform module and the PrivateLink NLB pattern to the shared drive (link below). For the production PrivateLink pattern we'll provide a TF module that builds an NLB in front of the service and registers target groups across AZs. That module includes health checks and autoscaling knobs.

Jared — great, thanks for the quick replies. Proposed next steps and owners:
1) Redwood to provision temporary S2S VPN (Rishi) — target by Tue EOD for basic traffic validation.
2) Acme firewall team to open TCP/443 + IPsec management ports to the POC ranges (Jared) — confirmation expected by Wed.
3) We will run a 10-day POC exercise capturing p50/p95 latencies, throughput, and error rates. Acceptance: p95 < 130ms and error rate < 1% for the POC window.
4) Post-POC review: decide between moving to PrivateLink (recommended for production) or keeping an NLB/peering approach. Karthik will produce a short cost delta for the two options.

I'll schedule a 30-minute kickoff tomorrow to walk through the POC checklist and handoffs. Thanks everyone — attaching the diagram and the connectivity matrix for reference.
